newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: OSCE hopes to bury differences at security summit.
newsitem.headline: OSCE hopes to bury differences at security summit.

text.p: European and North American leaders hope to declare agreement on Tuesday on what path to take towards peace in the 21st century, despite divisions which marred the first day of a security summit.

Leaders of more than 50 nations in the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) want to end their two-day meeting in Lisbon with a document setting out their vision of security, human rights and democracy across Europe.
But differences over NATO's expansion plans overshadowed the hopeful speeches on Monday and a row between Armenia and Azerbaijan could yet block the final declaration.

The divisions, and concern among the assembled leaders over Serbia's threat to crack down on opposition protesters gathering daily on the streets of Belgrade, highlighted the problems which accompany the hope as Europe braces for the next century.

"As we approach the new century, it is more important than ever that we build together a peaceful...region where all our nations and individuals feel secure," the leaders said in a draft version of the final declaration.

"We are determined to learn from the tragedies of the past and to translate our vision of a cooperative future into reality by creating a common security space free of dividing lines in which all states are equal partners."
The high point of Monday was an agreement on a new round of arms control talks that would adapt and extend a Cold War-era agreement cutting conventional forces in Europe.

The leaders were also united by fears that Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic will use force against protesters seeking his resignation. Rump Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, did not attend because its OSCE membership has been suspended.
International peace coordinator Carl Bildt urged Milosevic to drop his threat to crush the protests.

"We welcome the OSCE's continuing focus on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Democratisation, independent media, free and fair elections are critical to fostering lasting stability in the area," the draft summit document said.
But it did not take long for Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to sound a discordant note at the meeting grouping leaders from Europe, the United States and Canada.

He said Moscow firmly opposed NATO's plans to take in countries of Eastern Europe which used to be in the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact, reiterating concerns that such expansion would threaten Russia's security.

U.S. Vice President Al Gore tried to ease Russia's fears, telling the summit that Moscow had nothing to fear from NATO. Polish President Alexander Kwasniewski was more blunt, saying Russia's thinking was shaped by the stereotypes of the Cold War.

"Moscow has trouble accepting that NATO's enlargement is a foregone conclusion," said Kwasniewski, whose country is top of the list for early NATO membership together with the Czech Republic and Hungary.

Only Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko came to Russia's support in opposing NATO enlargement. But he found himself under attack for his record on democracy, particularly over a referendum last month which approved sweeping powers for him.
Unruffled, Lukashenko hit back calmly but hard. "It would be counterproductive to try to exert pressure on us or try to interfere in our internal affairs," he said.

The dispute which could torpedo the final summit declaration was played out on the fringes of the summit by Armenia and Azerbaijan over Nagorno-Karabakh, an enclave which has an Armenian majority but is surrounded by Azeri territory.
Azerbaijan wants its territorial integrity reaffirmed in the final document, but Armenia is opposed to such a reference.
Either Armenia or Azerbaijan could block the final communique because every OSCE member has the right to a veto.
The situation would be reminiscent of the last OSCE summit, in Budapest in 1994, which was wrecked by a row on the NATO issue and differences over Bosnia.
